So, Diego. What do you enjoy most about dermatology?
I enjoy following a patient over several years. With chronic conditions you see the whole story, not one visit.

I have interviewed international graduates for eleven years, and I can usually tell in the first five minutes who is going to do well, and it is not about accent. It is about verbs. When I ask what somebody enjoys about dermatology, the weak answer is a list of nouns: research, patients, procedures. The strong answer is a sentence with a verb in it. I enjoy following a patient for years. I enjoy explaining a diagnosis that frightened somebody. You can hear a person in that. The second thing I listen for is honesty about weaknesses. Everybody plans to improve. Very few people admit having a real problem. If you tell me you tend to avoid presenting cases because you are nervous in English, and then you tell me exactly what you have decided to do about it, I believe you. If you tell me you have no weaknesses, I stop listening. And the third thing. I always ask what you would do if you did not know an answer on the ward. The candidates I remember say something like: I would admit not knowing, I would look it up, and I would go back to the patient before the end of the day. That is the whole interview, really. Enjoying something, admitting something, and planning to do something about it.

For my first year of preparation I studied the wrong way, and I did it very efficiently. I kept reading the same review book, cover to cover, three times. I remember feeling productive every evening. What I was actually doing was avoiding the thing I was bad at, which was answering questions under time pressure. A friend who had passed the year before asked me one question: how many practice blocks have you done? None. I had planned to start them after the third reading. So I stopped reading the book and started doing questions, forty a day, timed, every day before work. The first two weeks were terrible. I risked failing every block, and I failed most of them. But I managed to see a pattern: I tended to change correct answers at the last minute. I decided to stop doing that, and I tried writing my first answer on paper before I clicked. It was a small thing. My score went up twelve points in a month. If somebody asks me now, I tell them it is worth reading less and answering more, and that the habit you are avoiding is probably the one you need.

Thank you for having me today. What I enjoy most is following a patient over several years. I tend to avoid presenting cases, because I get nervous in English. So I have decided to present one case every week this year. After Step 3, I plan to apply for a dermatology residency. I look forward to hearing from you.
